title: Grameen Bank: banking on trust instead of collateral
summary: Economics professor Muhammad Yunus lent the equivalent of $27 from his own pocket to 42 bamboo stool makers in the village of Jobra, who were trapped buying materials from moneylenders. That experiment became Grameen Bank (1983), built on group lending, weekly meetings and the belief that the poor are creditworthy.
results: Grew to serve roughly 9–10 million members, about 97% of them women
Pioneered solidarity-group lending now copied in dozens of countries
Yunus and the bank received the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize
Popularised the idea that repayment discipline can replace collateral
lesson: Social collateral (the group) can substitute for physical collateral — but it requires disciplined, high-touch operations.
source: Grameen Bank publications; Nobel Prize records

title: BRAC: from relief agency to the world's largest NGO lender
summary: BRAC began as a relief organisation after Bangladesh's independence war and gradually built one of the world's largest microfinance operations, pairing credit with health, education and livelihood programmes — the 'microfinance-plus' model.
results: Serves millions of borrowers across Bangladesh, mostly rural women
Demonstrated that combining credit with training can deepen impact
Its 'graduation' approach for the ultra-poor has been adapted in dozens of countries
Operates bKash, one of the world's largest mobile money services (as majority owner)
lesson: Credit works best as one tool in a wider development toolkit, especially for the poorest households.
source: BRAC annual reports; CGAP case studies

title: BancoSol: the NGO that became a commercial microfinance bank
summary: BancoSol was the world's first private commercial bank dedicated exclusively to microfinance. It grew out of the NGO PRODEM, proving microcredit could be run profitably under full banking regulation — and attract commercial capital instead of donor money.
results: Showed microfinance could fund itself from savings and capital markets
Sparked a wave of 'transformations' from NGO to regulated bank worldwide
Kept focus on micro-entrepreneurs in El Alto and other urban markets
Demonstrated the trade-offs of commercialisation (growth vs depth of outreach)
lesson: Regulation and commercial funding can scale microfinance — but mission drift is a real, manageable risk.

title: Equity Bank: from building society to East Africa's banking giant
summary: Founded as a small building society, Equity re-invented itself in the 1990s to serve low-income Kenyans whom banks ignored — no minimum balances, branches in rural towns, and later agency banking and mobile services (Equitel).
results: Grew into one of Africa's largest banks by customer numbers (well over 10 million customers)
Proved a mass-market, low-margin model can be highly profitable
Pioneered agency banking through local shops, slashing distribution costs
Became a template for inclusive banking in Africa
lesson: Designing products around low-income customers' realities beats repackaging rich-country banking.
source: Equity Bank Group reports; IFC case studies

title: Compartamos: microfinance's most controversial IPO
summary: Mexico's Compartamos went from NGO to regulated bank to a stock-market listing that made early investors large returns. Its high interest rates and the IPO windfall ignited a global debate: how much profit is acceptable when lending to the poor?
results: Reached millions of borrowers and proved massive demand for microcredit
Its IPO triggered an industry-wide reckoning on pricing and mission
Spurred interest-rate transparency initiatives such as MFTransparency
Became the canonical case study in 'mission drift' debates
lesson: Commercial success and social mission can coexist — but pricing and governance decide whether clients share in the gains.
source: Academic case studies (e.g. Stanford GSB); public filings

title: Kiva: crowdfunding microloans from a laptop
summary: Kiva let anyone lend $25 to micro-entrepreneurs worldwide through online profiles. Behind the scenes, funds flow through local field partners (MFIs), which pre-finance the loans — a structure often misunderstood as direct person-to-person lending.
results: Channelled well over a billion dollars in crowdfunded microloans to millions of borrowers
Brought a new generation of small lenders into financial inclusion
Taught the sector hard lessons about transparent communication
Expanded into 0%-interest direct lending experiments (Kiva US, Kiva Protocol)
lesson: Storytelling can mobilise capital at scale, but honesty about how money actually moves matters.

title: M-Pesa: the phone that became a bank account
summary: M-Pesa turned basic mobile phones into money wallets, using a vast network of airtime agents as cash-in/cash-out points. It began as a microfinance loan-repayment tool and exploded into East Africa's dominant payment rail — later adding savings (M-Shwari) and credit products.
results: Grew to tens of millions of users across several African countries
Moved a large share of Kenya's GDP through mobile transactions
Lifted many households' access to finance, documented in MIT research (Suri & Jack)
Became the reference model for mobile money worldwide
lesson: Distribution is everything: trusted local agents plus simple phones beat bank branches for reach.

title: Ørsted: the oil-and-gas company that sold itself into wind
summary: DONG Energy was a fossil-fuel utility. Over a decade it divested oil, gas and coal, renamed itself Ørsted, and bet the company on offshore wind — financed through green bonds, project partnerships and farm-downs of stakes in wind farms to recycle capital.
results: Became the world's largest offshore-wind developer by capacity
Regularly ranked among the most sustainable energy companies (Corporate Knights)
Showed capital markets will fund a credible transition story at scale
Provided the template utilities worldwide now cite in transition plans
lesson: Transition finance works when strategy, assets and funding all move in the same direction — half-measures convince no one.
source: Ørsted annual reports; Corporate Knights rankings

title: M-KOPA: pay-as-you-go solar for off-grid homes
summary: M-KOPA sells solar home systems to off-grid households on daily mobile-money instalments, with the system locking remotely if payments stop. It fused microfinance, mobile money and clean energy into one product — PAYGo solar.
results: Connected millions of homes to solar power across several African markets
Built credit histories for customers with no formal records
Showed asset-finance can electrify off-grid households profitably
Expanded from solar into smartphones and electric bikes on the same model
lesson: The pay-as-you-go structure turns an unaffordable $200 asset into an affordable daily habit — financing is the product.
source: M-KOPA public impact reports; GOGLA sector data

title: Triodos Bank: banking that publishes every loan it makes
summary: Triodos was founded to lend only to projects with positive social, environmental or cultural impact — organic farms, wind co-ops, schools, social housing. It publishes every organisation it lends to, making transparency its brand.
results: Grew into a mid-sized European bank financing hundreds of sustainable projects
Co-created the Global Alliance for Banking on Values
Proved values-based banking can be stable and profitable across crises
Set the transparency bar mainstream banks are now pushed toward
lesson: Radical transparency is a viable business strategy, not just an ethical luxury.
